title: Machine learning reveals distinct neural control of morning and evening body-temperature rhythms in Drosophila
summary: The February 2026 THERM-D preprint used learned fly localization in camera images to track temperature-preference rhythms over several days. Body temperature was inferred from flies’ positions on a temperature gradient, rather than directly measured by thermal imaging, and targeted genetic perturbations implicated CRYPTOCHROME-negative clock neurons in the morning temperature rise without the same evening effect. Author-maintained software documents a trained YOLOv8 object detector supporting fly localization. These are Drosophila findings, not an established human mechanism; the later November 2026 journal version is distinct from the preprint summarized here.
ai_technology: YOLOv8 object-detection model in the THERM-D computer-vision workflow
organization: University of California, Davis; University of Würzburg; Okayama University

evidence.tested: Continuous computer-vision BTR measurement with genetic clock disruption and targeted Gal4 neuronal manipulations in Drosophila; control comparisons tested separate morning/evening circuits.
evidence.unknown: Generalization beyond Drosophila and human relevance are unestablished. Preferred ambient position is a body-temperature proxy for these small ectotherms; the exact frozen preprint software/model snapshot was not identified.
evidence.ai_role: The preprint uses learned camera-image localization to derive fly positions and temperature-preference time courses. The version-linked author software release identifies a trained YOLOv8 detector and ONNX bounding-box inference; exact frozen weights used for the February preprint were not established.

source_review.scope: Original February2026 preprint XML: assay, fly-position/temperature proxy, neuronal perturbation results, affiliations and dates; bioRxiv API v1 history; author v0.1.0 README and ONNX detection code. Final journal metadata used only for version distinction.
